To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) leaf expansion in northern red oak ( Quercus rubr a) was associated with a decrease in leaf water potential ( Ψ L ) and leaf stomatal conductance per unit area (g s ), and 2) the hydraulic conductance of a seedling ( G ) was closely correlated with g s.

the leaf area, root length and stomatal conductance per unit area of northern red oak seedlings grown under controlled, favourable conditions increased during the first three polycyclic growth cycles and that these increases occurred in parallel with changes in hydraulic plant conductance.
the stomatal conductance of northern red oak seedlings decreased as leaf area increased during polycyclic shoot growth, and that the plant conductance per leaf area decreased in a similar fashion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of leaf growth on leaf water relations.
the role of stomata in controlling plant water relations during growth.
water transport in woody plants
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the stomatal conductance and hydraulic conductance per unit of leaf area of northern red oak seedlings are both highly responsive to leaf area, and that the two conductances are closely correlated during the early phases of polycyclic growth.

the changes in g s, Ψ L and G observed during the first three polycyclic growth periods in northern red oak seedlings grown under controlled conditions appear to be a consequence of the combined effects of the changes in the area of leaf surfaces and the area of root surfaces.

the changes in g s during the polycyclic growth cycle of northern red oak were primarily the result of changes in leaf area and that the changes in G were primarily the result, directly or indirectly, of the changes in g L.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
G, Ψ L and g s of northern red oak seedlings change in concert during the polycyclic growth cycle and that this pattern is likely a general feature of deciduous angiosperms.
the hydraulic conductance of a seedling is a function of its size and the size of its leaves.
the hydraulic conductance per unit area of a northern red oak seedling is relatively constant and that the stomatal conductance of the seedling's leaves is a function of its hydraulic conductance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the hydraulic conductance of a seedling increases with increasing leaf area and that this increase in conductance is sufficient to maintain leaf water potentials at levels that are relatively constant over time.
the hydraulic properties of red oak leaves change in a way that helps to keep the water potential of red oak leaves relatively constant during the first three cycles of leaf flush and expansion.
the stomata of red oak leaves are not tightly regulated during leaf expansion.
